me: Adjective, Accusative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word describes a person who is greedy, especially one pursuing dishonest gain. It points to a corrupt desire for money or advantage rather than faithful, honorable service. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in descriptions of people expected to show trustworthy character. The word therefore identifies greed connected with improper profit, not merely ordinary care in providing for needs. Its meaning is especially relevant when Scripture evaluates leaders and servants, warning that a desire for dishonest gain is incompatible with their responsibility.

d: Pollution, perhaps a polluted thing (especially of food).
me: Noun, Genitive, Plural, Neuter

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “defilement” or “pollution,” referring to something regarded as contaminated or made unclean. It is a term for a condition of impurity rather than a person, place, or object by itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Acts 15:20, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding passage. The wording points to defilement as a condition to be avoided.

gl: one who takes care of a vineyard

me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “a vine-worker,” someone who takes care of a vineyard. It refers to a person responsible for tending grapevines and the vineyard where they grow. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 13:7, so its normal meaning is represented by that single occurrence. Its focus is the worker’s role in caring for cultivated vines, rather than the vineyard itself. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: To act like a man, to be brave.
me: Verb, Present, middle or passive depoNent, iMperative, second, Plural

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to act courageously” or “to act like a man.” It describes a call to show courage and resolve rather than fear or weakness. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 16:13. Its wording presents courageous action as something a person is urged to do. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific situation and force of that instruction.

The central idea is deliberate opposition: a person places themselves against another’s will, direction, or conduct. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is physical birth or the producing of something in a broader sense. Its two occurrences are James 1:15 and James 1:18.

d: To grind or gnash, as with the teeth for rage or pain.
me: Verb, Imperfect, Active, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This verb means “to gnash,” describing the forceful grinding or clenching of the teeth. It expresses an intense physical reaction, often associated with anger, distress, or hostility, though the precise force depends on the surrounding passage. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 7:54. The word therefore focuses on the outward action of grinding the teeth rather than naming a separate emotion by itself.

The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a person or people identified as Galilean.

Its meaning is direct and focused: something or someone is received. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 6:17. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not part of this word-level description, the precise force of receiving there belongs to that passage’s context.

d: To wrap up, roll up in (something), wind in.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek verb means “to enwrap” or “to wrap in”: it describes the action of covering or enclosing something by wrapping it. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Mark 15:46. Because the word is an action verb, it focuses on what someone does rather than naming the covering itself. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the act of wrapping something around or within another covering.

Its basic meaning remains straightforward: a goat, a domesticated animal familiar in biblical settings.

Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a governing ruler or official.

me: Noun, Genitive, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “nail” or “nails,” referring to the hard metal object used to fasten something. It names a tangible object rather than an action, quality, or feeling. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, both within John 20:25. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains straightforward: one or more nails.

The word appears 12 times in the Greek New Testament, each in a different verse. Its exact emphasis—whether adding the speaker to others or highlighting the speaker’s participation—comes from the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the joining of “I” with what has already been said.

d: A cellar, vault, hidden place, crypt.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word refers to a cellar or another hidden place, especially a location where something can be kept out of sight. Its central idea is concealment rather than an ordinary open room or public area. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Luke 11:33, and is rendered “cellar” there. The broader gloss “hidden place” also helps show that the word can describe a concealed location generally, while “cellar” gives its concrete sense in that occurrence.

d: Mahalaleel or Maleleel, one of the ancestors of Jesus.
me: Noun, Genitive, Singular, Masculine, Person

e.t: Mahalalel is a personal name, referring to a particular individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs once, at Luke 3:37. Because it is a name, its meaning here is chiefly identification: it distinguishes Mahalalel from the other people named in the surrounding record. The name itself does not provide enough information to describe the person’s character, role, or significance beyond identifying him.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “evening” or “in the evening,” referring to the later part of the day as daylight fades and night approaches. It functions as a time expression, helping identify when something happens rather than describing a person, object, or action. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew and Mark. Its basic meaning remains consistent across these occurrences: it points to evening time. The precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 23:3. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and conversation, but the word itself points plainly to unlawful conduct or treating the law as something to be violated.

It is used when someone wants to know where something comes from or where it is located, rather than naming the place itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 29 times across 26 verses, showing repeated use as a question or location-related expression. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding words and passage.

d: To announce or preach beforehand, announce by herald.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Participle, Genitive, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “to announce” or “to preach beforehand.” It describes proclaiming a message in advance, making it known before the event or fulfillment being announced. As a verb, it focuses on the act of publicly declaring something ahead of time rather than merely mentioning it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 13:24. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic idea is advance proclamation.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “bird” or “birds,” referring to a winged creature. It names living things identified by wings, rather than a person, place, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 15:39. Its precise role there depends on the surrounding passage, whose text is needed to explain the verse-level emphasis. Its central idea is shared participation in conduct that presents a false appearance, with the emphasis on joining others in that behavior. The surrounding verse supplies the specific situation in which this action occurred.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Hebrews 11:35. It is rendered as tortured there, agreeing with its central sense. The word can describe either undergoing torture or carrying it out; its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context.

d: Jacinth, a precious stone of the color of hyacinth.

e.t: This word names a “hyacinth,” also rendered “jacinth.” It refers to a particular named object rather than an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Revelation 21:20. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, its exact role in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself. Its basic meaning, however, is the name of the substance or object called a hyacinth or jacinth.

As a Greek New Testament word, it appears once, in Acts 6:11. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning points to covertly urging or prompting someone rather than openly making a request or argument.

The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Matthew and once in Luke. Both occurrences belong to the same saying about how people characterized Jesus in contrast with John the Baptist, but the word itself chiefly identifies a person as a glutton. Its exact force in either verse is understood from the surrounding passage.
